# Paying for inference twice

## Where we got to

Particle MCMC gave us the posterior for the SEITL model — at a price:

- one particle filter per likelihood evaluation
- hundreds of thousands of evaluations per chain
- hours of compute

::: {.fragment}
And the answer applies to [exactly one dataset]{.alert}.
:::

## The same model, again

A second island. A different reporting schedule. The same outbreak truncated at
week three.

::: {.fragment}
Every one of those is a fresh chain, from scratch, at full cost.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Nothing we computed the first time helps us the second time.
:::

## Variational inference got us halfway

In the previous session we replaced *sampling* with *optimisation*: pick a family
$q(\theta)$, then optimise until it is close to the posterior.

::: {.fragment}
Much faster. But $q(\theta)$ was fitted to **one** dataset.

Change the data and you re-run the optimisation.
:::

::: {.fragment}
What if we optimised something that works for [any]{.alert} dataset?
:::

# Amortised inference

## The idea

Stop treating the posterior as a thing to compute, and start treating it as a
[function to learn]{.alert}:

$$q_\phi(\theta \mid y) \approx p(\theta \mid y)$$

::: {.fragment}
Train it on simulations, then apply it to real data.
:::

## Training data is free

We already have a simulator. Use it to generate pairs:

$$\theta_i \sim p(\theta), \qquad y_i \sim p(y \mid \theta_i)$$

::: {.fragment}
Then fit a conditional density estimator by maximum likelihood:

$$\min_\phi \; -\sum_i \log q_\phi(\theta_i \mid y_i)$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Over draws from the joint $p(\theta)p(y \mid \theta)$, the minimiser of that loss
is the [true posterior]{.alert} [@papamakarios2016].
:::

## So what is it, really?

Not a new model. Not a new inferential target.

::: {.fragment}
The same posterior, for the same mechanistic model, with the same priors —
reached by **regression on simulations** instead of by sampling.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The neural network replaces the **sampler**, not the model. $R_0$ still means
$R_0$.
:::

## Normalising flows {.smaller}

We need a $q_\phi(\theta \mid y)$ we can both **evaluate** (to train) and
**sample from** (to use).

::: {.fragment}
A normalising flow is an invertible network mapping a standard normal to
something complicated, conditioned on the data:

$$z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \qquad \theta = T_\phi(z; y)$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Invertible with a tractable Jacobian, so the change-of-variables formula gives
the density directly.
:::

## Amortisation

Training is expensive and happens [once]{.alert}.

::: {.fragment}
After that, a posterior is a single forward pass: **milliseconds**, no MCMC, no
further simulation.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The cost moves from *per dataset* to *once, ever*. That is the whole trade.
:::

# How this differs from VI

## Two kinds of optimisation {.smaller}

|  | Variational inference | Neural posterior estimation |
|---|---|---|
| Optimises | $q(\theta)$, one dataset | $q_\phi(\theta \mid y)$, all datasets |
| Divergence | reverse KL | forward KL, averaged over $y$ |
| Fails by being | too **narrow** | too **wide** |
| Needs | the likelihood | only the simulator |
| New dataset | re-optimise | free |

::: {.fragment}
NPE is, in effect, *amortised* variational inference with the KL reversed.
:::

## Why the failure modes differ

Reverse KL is [mode-seeking]{.alert} — it would rather cover one mode well than
spread thin. Hence the too-narrow mean-field posteriors you saw.

::: {.fragment}
Forward KL is [mass-covering]{.alert} — it is penalised for putting low density
where the truth has mass. Hence posteriors that err wide.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Erring wide is usually the safer failure.
:::

## The amortisation gap

The estimator must work for **every** dataset the prior can produce.

::: {.fragment}
So on any single dataset it will be worse than a bespoke fit.

More training shrinks the gap. It does not close it.
:::

# Making it work

## Ragged surveillance {.smaller}

Real data is not a tidy rectangle: locations start reporting at different times,
days are missed, sites are surveyed twice in seven years.

::: {.fragment}
But a neural network needs [fixed-length]{.alert} input.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Fix a grid, then add a **binary mask** saying which points were observed
[@wang2024]:

$$x = [\; \underbrace{y \odot m}_{\text{zero-filled}} \;|\; \underbrace{m}_{\text{the mask}} \;]$$
:::

## Why the mask is not optional

Zero-filling alone is ambiguous.

::: {.fragment}
Is a zero on day 12 a day when nobody reported, or a day when genuinely zero
cases were reported?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Those imply very different things about $\theta$. The mask is what distinguishes
them — the padding carries no information at all.
:::

## One network, every schedule

Draw a **random mask for every training example**.

::: {.fragment}
The network then learns $p(\theta \mid y, m)$ — a posterior conditioned on the
observation schedule itself.
:::

::: {.fragment}
So we can condition on schedules we invent *after* training. That is how you
price a surveillance design without refitting anything.
:::

## Never reuse a simulation

Neural networks usually overfit a fixed training set — validation loss bottoms
out, then climbs.

::: {.fragment}
A SEITL outbreak takes well under a millisecond to simulate.

So: draw a [fresh batch for every gradient step]{.alert}. No example is ever seen
twice, and overfitting becomes impossible by construction.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Costs about 5% extra per step — free, but only because the simulator is fast.
:::

# What it costs

## Checking the answer

There is no $\hat{R}$, no effective sample size, no trace plot to stare at.

::: {.fragment}
Instead: **simulation-based calibration** [@talts2018]. Draw from the prior,
simulate, fit, and record the rank of the truth among the posterior draws.

Calibrated $\Rightarrow$ those ranks are uniform.
:::

## The silent failure {.smaller}

MCMC on a badly specified model gives you visibly bad fits and pathological
diagnostics.

::: {.fragment}
A trained flow will map data it has never seen anything like onto a tidy,
narrow, [confident and wrong]{.alert} posterior — with nothing to flag it
[@hermans2022].
:::

::: {.fragment}
Prior and posterior predictive checks are your main guard. They matter more here
than they did for MCMC.
:::

## When to use which

- **NUTS** — tractable, differentiable likelihood, one dataset
- **PMMH** — stochastic model, exact, one dataset, you have hours
- **VI** — need speed on one dataset, can live with narrow intervals
- **NPE** — same model, many datasets, or many hypothetical designs

::: {.fragment}
For a one-off fit, use PMMH. For the hundredth fit of the same model,
amortisation wins.
:::
